# Is it ok to start the car with my GPS, cell phone, etc. plugged into the 12V port?

The concern about starting a vehicle with USB devices or auxiliary power adapters plugged into the 12V cigarette lighter port stems from the electrical event known as inrush current. When you turn the ignition keyâor press the start buttonâthe starter motor engages. This component is essentially a high-torque DC motor that requires hundreds of amps to overcome engine compression and begin rotation. During this brief window, the battery voltage can sag significantly, often dropping from a healthy 12.6V down to 9V or lower depending on the load and battery health.

The fear is that this rapid voltage dip triggers a brownout within your connected electronics. If a GPS unit or smartphone has a poorly regulated power supply, it might reset, reboot, or suffer hardware damage due to voltage transients coupled with ground loops. While modern consumer electronics are generally robust against minor fluctuations, the physics of automotive electrical systems do create a hostile environment for sensitive components during cranking.

To understand why this happens, we have to look at how these devices manage power. Most USB-C chargers and car adapters use switching power supplies (SMPS) that expect a relatively stable input voltage range, typically 9V to 16V for USB-PD or standard 5V/12V inputs. When the engine starts, the battery voltage doesn't just dip; it can momentarily spike in noise as the alternator begins to spin and regulate voltage. This creates a scenario where your device sees a noisy input while its internal logic tries to maintain stability.

In a worst-case scenario involving older electronics or cheaply made adapters, the power supply's capacitors may discharge too quickly to buffer this drop, causing the device to reset. However, if you plug a device directly into the USB port of a modern navigation unit or phone, those devices often have their own internal battery and sophisticated power management ICs (PMIC) designed to handle automotive noise. In these cases, the risk of permanent damage is negligible, but the annoyance of a reboot remains a valid trade-off.

There is also the question of the "surge" mentioned in older advice. Some theories suggest that connecting a load before the alternator is fully online creates a high-current draw that stresses the starter motor or drains the battery excessively. Mathematically, if you have a 60Ah battery and a starter drawing 300A for 2 seconds, you are pulling 1800Coulombs of charge instantly. If your GPS draws an additional 2A during this time, it is technically drawing from that same depleted pool. While the energy difference is small in absolute terms (a few Joules), the voltage sag caused by the combined load can be more severe than if the devices were unplugged, potentially pushing sensitive analog components below their minimum operating threshold.

If you are building a custom dashboard integration or modifying a vehicle's infotainment system, the engineering approach changes slightly. You would design your power distribution board to isolate sensitive electronics from the main battery bus during cranking. This often involves using diodes to create an OR-ing configuration or ensuring that non-essential loads are switched off via relays controlled by the ignition signal before the starter engages.

For the average driver with a standard setup, the advice to unplug devices is more about preserving data integrity and preventing annoying reboots than preventing catastrophic hardware failure. If your GPS unit freezes every time you start the car, that is a clear indicator that its power supply cannot handle the automotive voltage dip. The solution isn't necessarily to buy a new device, but perhaps to ensure it has a decent buffer capacitor or to use a dedicated battery pack for the accessory if the vehicle's alternator regulation is sluggish.

Ultimately, while the "old wives' tale" label is often applied to this myth, there is enough electrical noise and voltage sag during cranking that unplugging sensitive devices is a prudent engineering practice. It isolates the variable of the starter motor's massive current draw from your delicate electronics. If you want to test the limits, try starting the car with a device plugged in and observe if it resets; if it does, your power supply design needs better filtering or buffering for that specific automotive environment.
